analysis.one_liner: Bans unlimited 'soft money' contributions to national political parties and tightens campaign finance disclosure rules.
analysis.headline: Introduced with bipartisan support from 45 House members, the campaign finance overhaul died in committee without a committee vote or a floor vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have barred national political party committees from raising or spending unlimited 'soft money' — donations that escaped federal contribution limits and disclosure rules. It would have required party committees to use regulated, disclosed funds for federal election activity, tightened disclosure of contributors and independent campaign spending, banned fundraising on federal property, limited campaign mail, and let House candidates volunteer to cap their own personal spending at $50,000. It was referred to four committees, sent to subcommittees, and never brought up again before that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary voters, who would learn who is paying for federal campaign activity and see party committees cut off from unlimited, undisclosed donations from corporations, unions, and wealthy individuals.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voters seeking disclosure of campaign money

how_it_helps.text: National party committees could no longer solicit, receive, or spend any funds outside the limits, prohibitions, and reporting requirements of federal campaign law [S2].

State and local party committees would have to use regulated, reported funds for federal election activity such as voter registration, get-out-the-vote drives, and ads mentioning federal candidates [S2].
Party committees would be barred from soliciting or directing money to tax-exempt 501(c) organizations, a common channel for unregulated political spending [S2].
Federal filings would have to be posted on the Internet within 24 hours, and donor identification thresholds would drop from $200 to $50 [S2].

Federal officials, including the President and Members of Congress, could not solicit political donations while in federal office space, and penalties for knowing and willful violations would double [S2].
The bill would strengthen the ban on foreign nationals' donations and prohibit campaign contributions from minors [S2].

analysis.who_pays: National party committees, which would lose the unlimited soft-money channel, and major donors who relied on it. Wealthy self-financed House candidates would face a $50,000 personal-spending cap if they opted into the voluntary program. Unions would have to run a procedure letting nonmember employees opt out of paying for political activity.

drawbacks.text: The bill raises the aggregate individual contribution limit from $25,000 to $30,000, letting the biggest donors give more through regulated channels [S2].

It leaves genuinely independent express-advocacy spending outside contribution limits — only subject to reporting — so money that does not coordinate with candidates could still be unlimited, though it must be disclosed [S2].

Its new 'express advocacy' definition would treat broadcast ads naming a candidate within 60 days of an election as regulated campaign speech, a rule critics viewed as burdening political speech, and the bill includes fast-track Supreme Court review anticipating constitutional challenges [S2].

Title V adds an unrelated labor provision requiring unions to let nonmember employees opt out of funding political activity, which backers of campaign finance reform criticized as a concession designed to win Republican votes [S2].
The $50,000 personal wealth limit, with a penalty tied to party coordinated spending, restricts candidates' ability to fund their own campaigns [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is straightforward: unlimited, loosely disclosed party 'soft money' would be replaced with regulated, disclosed contributions, and donor disclosure thresholds would drop sharply. The costs are real but modest — a higher overall limit for the largest individual donors, an aggressive definition of campaign advertising that drew constitutional objections, and an unrelated union-fee provision bundled in for political reasons. On balance the bill's main effect is to shrink the special-interest money channel rather than expand it.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to four House committees in March 1998 and to two subcommittees in April, and it never came out of committee or reached the floor before the Congress ended in January 1999.

narrative.text: Rep. Christopher Shays (R-CT) introduced the bill on March 19, 1998 with Rep. Martin Meehan and 13 other original cosponsors from both parties [S1].
The bill was referred to four committees: House Oversight (the lead committee), Education and the Workforce, Government Reform and Oversight, and Judiciary [S1].
In April 1998 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Government Management, Information and Technology and the Subcommittee on Employer-Employee Relations [S5].
No committee ever reported the bill, no floor vote was ever held, and the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999 with the bill still pending in committee [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: National party committees and the corporations, unions, and wealthy donors who continued giving them unlimited, lightly disclosed soft money after the bill died. Members of both parties kept that fundraising channel until a similar law passed in 2002.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Party committees and big soft-money donors

for.name: Rep. Christopher Shays
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Bipartisan Campaign Reform Act of 1998 in the House on March 19, 1998.

for.name: Rep. Martin Meehan
for.what_they_did: Joined Shays as the Democratic lead when the bill was introduced, making the reform bipartisan from the start.

for.name: Mrs. Roukema and other original cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors at introduction; the bill ultimately drew 45 cosponsors, 37 Democrats and 8 Republicans.

against.name: House Oversight Committee
against.role: Lead committee of referral (chaired by a Republican)
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to a subcommittee on March 30, 1998 and never reported it out; the bill died there.

against.name: Speaker Newt Gingrich
against.what_they_did: Under House rules, the Speaker controlled whether and when the bill would be scheduled for floor action; it was never scheduled in 1998, and House Republican leadership was widely reported to have resisted bringing campaign finance reform to a vote.

sides.party_line_note: Support for the bill was bipartisan at sponsorship — 37 of its 45 cosponsors were Democrats and 8 were Republicans [S4] — but no roll-call vote ever occurred because the bill never left committee.

industries.note: The bill would cut off their unlimited soft-money fundraising by requiring all federal election activity to run through regulated, disclosed funds, and would bar party donations to tax-exempt groups. Losing this channel is exactly what campaign finance reform aims to take from parties, and it is also where ordinary voters' disclosure interest runs against the parties' fundraising interest.

industries.industry: Major campaign donors and special-interest givers
industries.note: Big donors would lose the ability to give unlimited soft money to party committees, though the bill partially offsets this by raising the aggregate individual limit from $25,000 to $30,000 [S2]. The donor interest in hiding the size and source of political giving runs against voters' interest in disclosure.

The bill would codify the Beck decision, requiring unions to run an objection procedure letting nonmember employees reduce payments that fund political activity unrelated to collective bargaining [S2]. Unions face modest compliance costs and some political-funding opt-outs, while the provision itself was added as part of a bipartisan package.

House candidates who opt in face a $50,000 cap on personal and family funds, with a monetary penalty if exceeded. For wealthy candidates the bill restricts spending their own money; for voters it limits the advantage of deep pockets.

Political ads within 60 days of an election would face stricter identification and disclosure requirements, including 'stand by your ad' audio and on-screen statements [S2]. Stations and ad makers face compliance costs; viewers get clearer information about who is paying.
